subject: history
title: Interpreting Protest Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll judge sources and weigh how change came in Britain — from below, from above, or both?
meta_desc: GCSE AQA History — interpretations of protest, reform and rights in Britain c.1170-present.
final_note: You weighed top-down reform against bottom-up protest as drivers of change in British rights.

concepts.def: 1688 overthrow of James II — secured parliamentary rule
1819 massacre of reform protesters in Manchester
Protest by smashing, marching or hunger strike
1807 trade abolished, 1833 slavery ended in Empire
Gay rights, race relations — won by 20th-c campaigns

walkthroughs.body_html:
Some argue change came when elites chose to give it.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688, the 1807 abolition of the slave trade, and the 1832 Great Reform Act were all passed by Parliament and the rich — not by mass revolt.

Others argue pressure from below mattered most.

The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 shocked elites. Peterloo in 1819 became a martyrdom. Chartists, unions and Suffragettes built mass campaigns that scared governments into reform.

From Magna Carta (1215) to the Equal Franchise Act (1928), rights expanded.

20th-century campaigns won race relations laws (1965, 1976) and gay rights (decriminalised in England 1967). Most historians see both push from below and concession from above at work.
